Lucia, before the review starts, remind me which team actually owns the release pipeline now.
The team that fixed the bottleneck in the review step owns it. It is the group we consolidated in March.
And who runs it day to day?
Priya, the engineer who designed the first version. She also mentors everyone we onboard.
Was that the group with the retention problem last year?
It was. The two teams whose turnover was highest last year are now the most stable in the division.
What changed?
One manager instead of three, and the workaround we used for six months has finally been retired. My counterpart in Dublin, who runs the same platform in Europe, is copying the model to scale it.

Let me introduce the group that owns this platform, because most of you have only seen their names on a slide. The engineer who designed the first version of the pipeline is Priya, and she now mentors every person we onboard. The bottleneck that used to slow every release was in the review step, and the team that fixed it did the work in eleven days. Our lab in Zurich, where the models are tested before release, has doubled its capacity this year. My counterpart in Dublin, who runs the same platform for the European market, reports exactly the numbers we do. And the two groups whose turnover was highest last year are now the most stable in the division, because we consolidated them into one team with a single manager. The workaround we used for six months has finally been retired. That is the group. Ask them anything.

Here is the test I give every candidate, and it takes two seconds. Say the sentence out loud, then take the clause away and listen to what is left. If the sentence still tells me exactly which person or which system you mean, the clause was extra information, so it needs commas around it, and you must use who or which, never that. My counterpart in Dublin, who joined last year, runs the same platform. Take that clause out and you still know who I mean. But if the sentence suddenly becomes vague, the clause was doing real work, so no commas at all. The engineer who built the pipeline has left. Take that clause out and nobody knows which engineer. One more thing. In an interview, most of your clauses will be the defining kind, because you are naming projects, teams and people that nobody in that room has ever heard of.
